prompt:
A densely annotated editorial infographic plate, drawn by hand in confident ink
line with light watercolour and gouache wash on bright warm-white paper.
Contour line varies in weight and is charcoal near-black. Dimensional but not
photographic: restrained hatching, subtle texture, believable volume, selective
shadow, clean uncluttered background. Every material reads as itself — dull grey
lead, unglazed earthenware, weathered timber, damp fibrous bark — and materials
that differ in the explanation look visibly different. Quiet palette of stone,
clay, wood, and metal tones over the warm-white ground, with one or two
desaturated accents that each keep a single meaning throughout the plate.
Contemporary editorial typography: one calm display face for the title, one
highly legible face for the many small labels, sentence case, crisply printed
and correctly spelled. Annotation is dense and disciplined — leader lines,
brackets, dimension marks, magnified inset circles, small side studies — laid
out so no two leaders cross. Asymmetric composition with about a quarter of the
page left quiet. Modern printing on clean stock: fresh, crisp, and unaged. The
only lettering anywhere on the plate is the title, the deck, the labels, and the
short notes. The words hero, drawing, figure, plate, inset, zone, band, strip,
trio, column, and cutaway describe the construction of the page and are never
lettered onto it, alone or in a phrase: no headings that name parts of the
layout, no percentages or
proportions of the page, no tags in brackets after a label or note, no sentence
describing the drawing or explaining what the reader is meant to see, no
signature, monogram, date, watermark, or credit line.

Title, set largest at the top left of the page: proof
Deck beneath it: Each page of rescued text is held up against a picture of the original, and only the scanner's mistakes are mended — the author's hand is never touched.

Hero: a proofreader's double lectern dominates the centre. On its left leaf stands a rendered photograph of an old book page, warm-toned and slightly foxed; on its right leaf, the same page as typed text. Between them a large comparing lens on an articulated arm spans both leaves, and within the lens a single line is shown twice — above, from the photograph, the word ſubſtance set in old type with long-s characters; below, in the typed copy, the garbled word fubftance being corrected to substance, the mended letters picked out in the accent colour. A note at the lens: the long s of old type, misread as f, is the classic wound.

Around the lectern, three short annotations attached to small marks on the typed leaf:
- a garbled cluster of letters smoothed into a word, captioned: only scanning damage is mended — broken letters, split words;
- the word colour standing untouched with a small protective bracket over it, captioned: the author's own spelling and grammar stand, however old;
- a faint pencilled margin note reading uncertain, tied to one doubtful correction, captioned: a correction the reader doubts is flagged for a human eye, never silently made.

Along the bottom, a modest procession: a short row of page cards moving left to right through the lectern's shadow, the mended ones carrying a small stitch mark, one very short card walking past unexamined, captioned — a near-empty page passes through untouched, and a page whose picture cannot be made keeps its old text and says so.

At the lower right corner, a small open ledger with a few modest sums entered, captioned: every page's reading is paid for and entered in the ledger.

One warm accent colour marks the mended letters, the stitch marks, and the lens frame; the lectern, pages, and photograph stay in ink and grey wash.
